focus_profile.learning_goal: 关注利率、保证利益、退保行为、新业务价值、长期负债和寿险战略。
tasks: 复盘一条寿险新闻对利率假设、退保率或新业务价值的影响。
写一段寿险产品利润来源拆解：利差、死差、费差、退保差。
记录一个值得跟踪的寿险公司战略动作。

daily_concept.definition: IFRS 17 下未赚利润的负债组成部分，随保险服务提供逐步释放。
daily_concept.exercise: 选一家上市险企，写出 CSM 变动可能来自新业务、经验差异、假设变更还是释放。

items.rss_description: Independent Agents - A Forward View Agent & Broker ITL Editorial Team Fri, 10/23/2026 - 13:36 Economic simulations now forecast fiscal health across 1,900 U.S. localities, helping agents anticipate consumer affordability shifts and community financial stress. October 23, 2026 Image Local agents swim in the waters around them, and while a rising tide lifts all boats, that sucking sound before a tsunami hits shore is a clear signal that locality risk is a constant. It's good to be lucky with a rising tide, but luck is not a strategy. Simulations of the world are a way to describe observed reality and anticipate change, and modeling the changing economic tides of every locality in America (call that a list with 1,900 locations) is a good way to both reflect on what has happened since COVID-19 and to help those agents see what's coming next. Modeling Communities Like We Model Weather We simulate weather daily to anticipate storm tracks and estimate damage. We simulate climate change with variation in sea level, flood plains, and riverbanks. We simulate fire spread, hail fall, straight-line wind… and so, too, we should simulate the local economies of 1,900 communities across America. In a consumer-driven economy, simulating how America spends is like watching a developing hurricane pattern off the shore – is it intensifying or waning, is it heading for land or staying off the coast, what amount of intrusion to interior geographies will a footprint create, and will there be additional risks set in motion as the dynamics unfold, including supply chain and demand patterns that may also be interrupted or surged? Affordability and Fiscal Health as Key Signals Just as a student loan may go unpaid if post-graduate incomes are low, the choices households and individuals make on debts to service and debts to default are mirrored at businesses, organizations, and local communities, cities, and municipalities. These local priorities of affordability affect decisions on risk transfer and affect premiums – agents sit amid it all. (See this article on a data source to predict financial health, going beyond the backward-looking credit reports that insurers use.) Affordability is a key signal, as is the fiscal health of a locality. When you combine these with the inflows and outflows of households and businesses, any agency can make a plan for the year or two ahead and set in motion a process for continually navigating their locales. Looking Backward: The Affordability Crisis People living in houses and driving cars work at businesses and spend money in their communities. Unsurprisingly, changes in the economies of those communities are both observable and predictable. That matters to local agents. Looking backward, hindsight is usually 20/20 – higher uninsured driver populations occurred where affordability was lowest. More UM/UIM claims drive insurance costs higher, and rates may go up even further. In an economic downswing, rising costs and flat to slow wage increases force more budget stress on consumers. Where job loss escalates stress, things twist up even faster. Not only do consumers decide not to be insured, but they also change other spending habits. More businesses fail when customers can no longer afford them. Collections of tax revenue suffer when high earners migrate away and when business activity slows or falters. Taxes suffer further when sales slump, and property values deteriorate. These can lead to cuts in community services, and spiral from there. Emerging Patterns: From Data Centers to Remote Work Independent agents, brokers of all sizes, carriers, wholesalers, specialty, excess, and MGA/MGUs all compete in these predictable localities. And predictions for consumers, businesses, and even the localities are proving their value in understanding and pricing risk. Some localities see changes that are from emerging patterns of life and risk, like hyperscale data centers. Other changes are more subtle, like a work-from-anywhere job landscape that allows high earners to live wherever they want. Or what happens when AI shifts work tasks in legacy workflows or creates new ways of working? Boomtowns to ghost towns and everything in between paint the map of America -- parcel-by-parcel, building-by-building, business-by-business, organization-by-organization, job-by-job, and so, too, insurance and risk management dynamics. Some things change very slowly, while others shift abruptly, but the profound effect of "work anywhere" from COVID may be the most significant overarching impact in our generation and the next. Anticipating Economic Consequences We anticipate sudden changes to life patterns in a variety of peril-driven scenarios – hurricane, tornado, fire, severe convective storm – as well as in environmental scenarios like sea level change, cyclical patterns like El Niño, and even major disruptions like power outages, transportation interruptions, and cyber interference. Anticipating economic consequences, especially shifts in contribution to cash flow in community capital assets and liabilities, is another risk in the underlying infrastructure where all the other risks interact. Thriving localities add services and amenities, which attract more growth. Dwindling localities lay off public workers and renegotiate long-term liabilities while trying to improve local revenues with more taxes and fees. Debt offerings and the ability to service debt obligations are then most comparable to Ernest Hemingway's famous line on personal bankruptcy – which happens "gradually, then suddenly." New Analytics for Local Planning Analytics now exist for consumers, businesses, and their communities across the 1,900 localities that make up the investable and insurable economies of America. This observability of a locality, its finances, its threats/opportunities, and its ability to service its debts and obligations is summed across the consumer and business mix of their constituents and forecast against those changing elements to portray current and future years' planning horizons. Local agents can take heed. Situations with imminent insolvency are expected to make certain choices, while growth-busting upside creates better problems. Adapting to Local Reality While agents can always relocate, they are more likely to need to adapt to their local reality. While premium forecasts and business mix are constantly used in distribution planning and customer appetite focus, the pace of change has accelerated inside of the existing process steps. Using a locality stress index along with existing forecasts and affordability measures will make agents smarter in their marketplaces and quicker to react to change. This means that in troubled areas, expect more business failures, lapses, and non-payment of premiums in a dwindling premium pattern, yet a rise in risk for fraud, theft, and malicious mischief, including a heavier threat of arson. This includes household stress, too, where skyrocketing base rates have pushed daily budgeting stress onto most households for car and homeowner insurance into an affordability squeeze where many drivers are underinsured, overcommitting to large deductibles, or going all the way to lapsing insurance entirely and becoming uninsured drivers. What does luck look like? A common quote from successful businesses – "It's better to be lucky, even if you're good." Never has that been more relevant than today, as changes in local luck have magnified in recent years. Some places have a deep downside – rising taxes, failing businesses, public service degradation, municipal financial stress, drops in quality of life generally, and the ensuing changes in household composition from thriving to just holding on. Some places have all sunshine -- growth in incomes, formation of new jobs, infrastructure improvements, and engaged public services. To live in an uninvestable locality is the hallmark of being unlucky. The endpoints are always locality-based. It is where people live, where businesses operate, and where municipal authorities administer. For an agent, the forward look in these markets is flat to down. Fewer businesses for fewer booming households means fewer insurable assets. Even if premiums rise and commissions float with them, the total insurance value opportunity won't be in a boom cycle. The larger concern is a doom cycle. Investors are aware of the general migration trend outlined in this recent Census article , whereby large metro areas are losing residents, while many smaller metro areas are growing. Details matter, and this is where data and analytics add critical value: High earners are migrating away from large metro areas in fiscally troubled states. They are migrating to small and mid-sized metro areas: Boise, Idaho; Frisco, Texas. High earners are responsible for the majority of personal and property taxes, new business formation, and capital investments. Scoring the 1,900 Localities Across the observed 1,900 cities, the municipalities, consumers, and businesses are scored based on their future fiscal viability and likelihood to default across a set of debts (everyday bills, credit cards, car loans, mortgages, business loans, pension commitments, municipal bonds, etc.). Ranked near the top of the list is St. George, Utah, with a short-term debt ratio of 0.31, which represents total liabilities divided by total assets. St. George is representative of 60 mostly mid-sized "under the radar" cities that have low legacy liabilities and sustainable budgets and are growing their populations with a healthy taxpayer base. This is where you can feel comfortable doing business for the long term. Lucky local agents! Then there are plenty of typical "middling" cities, with budgets that are not sustainable over the long term due to underfunded pension and benefits liabilities. Steady as she goes for the next few years. On the other side of the scale – consider a poster child for fiscal mismanagement to the extent it appears on a list titled Uninvestable Cities. These cities are laying off public sector workers today as they struggle with revenue shortfalls. Most of these cities meet the technical definition of insolvency. They appear to have accelerating financial deterioration over the next 24 months, resulting in a highly likely outright fiscal crisis. Envision trying to do business in a city where high earners (lowest risk, rational decision-makers) are leaving. The businesses are shuttering, as well. New business formation is almost non-existent. The city struggles to fund basic services, while raising taxes. The residual population has lower FICO scores. Crime, including costly fraud, rises. The Resilience of Independent Agents Every year another study predicts the demise of independent agents. They are getting too old; they can't scale to digital; they can't compete with changing technology… add in AI. Yet every year independent agents remain a dominant force in commercial insurance and have never failed to impress in personal lines. Watch how they adapt across 1,900 localities as a way to keep insuring America. ADDITIONAL THOUGHTS PARKING LOT What has changed is almost everything all at once. Blame it on remote work options, but look at how many high-earner households opt to relocate for better taxes, better weather, better schools, better anything. Blame it on migration, but the businesses and services they need will follow them, while the ones that used to serve them will feel the loss. Blame it on anything you like, but the undeniable facts are that no one relocates to a state; they move to a specific location. The imbalances from losing localities to gaining localities are seen in shifts in income, housing, business formations/failures, and municipal financial resilience. To assess health, a current approach ties to the capital markets where municipalities trade their debt. Using a locality lens, it is possible to observe the condition of consumers, businesses, and municipalities. With modern data and analytics, we can track changes over time. Did all three (consumer, business, municipality) improve, stay the same, or deteriorate in the last few years? What is the effect of these local changes, and how fast are changes now occurring? What is in store for the next couple of years? The US is in the early stages of an economic transformation, by locality, and that means insurance agents have both local threats and opportunities. Like Detroit filing Chapter 9 bankruptcy in 2013, it is conceivable that other major cities may follow suit. No city is immune to stress in changing local economies, and dozens of large municipalities have a reckoning coming. The tax base within these cities (high-earner consumers and meaningful business tax bases) is departing at rates never seen before. Marty Ellingsworth

The tax base within these cities (high-earner consumers and meaningful business tax bases) is departing at rates never seen before. Marty Ellingsworth

items.title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.original_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_description: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer? AI & Machine Learning ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:19 Blocking Meta's AI agent on your website won't stop it from calling. Insurers need a plan to handle these calls. October 22, 2026 Image A consumer's AI agent can now call an insurer and ask for a quote. The possibility of such calls leaves carriers with two bad options: putting a licensed person on the line with a machine, or risk hanging up on a real person. Both options are wrong. There's a third. The AI phone calls are already happening. Reuters reported that people using Meta's Muse, the personal AI agent launched in the U.S. this past September, can have it call businesses to book appointments, check inventory or get quotes from contractors. A Meta employee testing this feature said an insurer kept hanging up on Muse after realizing it was an AI caller. At InsureTech Connect in Las Vegas, Steve Rullo, who is Guardian Life's chief digital and technology officer, told Insurance Business , "We are already seeing providers calling in for verification of benefits with AI." He described healthcare providers using AI to verify patient benefits, often for an entire list of patients in a single call. The Debate Is About Websites Since Muse launched, carriers and marketplaces have been deciding whether to allow it access. Insurify quickly blocked Muse, saying it "risks stripping carrier quotes of critical contextual information." Co-CEO Giorgos Zacharia explained, "A quote without its context is not a fair comparison. It is a number." Shortly afterward, Kin announced that it would let Muse crawl its site so customers can shop for quotes , and Zebra announced an integration the following day. Employers, a workers' compensation insurer, told Dig-In it doesn't allow third-party AI agents like Muse to access its operational systems or customer data. Each of those decisions is about access to a website or system. None of them covers phone calls, and blocking Muse online won't stop it from calling. I expect insurers will get a lot more of these calls. Handled the old way, they're a cost. Handled well, every one is a quote in front of a real shopper. That's where the real opportunities are. The Talking Is About 5% of the Value The answer is simple: AI for AI, humans for humans. Let AI answer calls from other AI, and let people answer calls from people. This way, a family dealing with a flooded basement won't be stuck on hold while a licensed agent talks to a bot. Most voice AI answers the phone, then sends the caller through a phone menu or to a person. That's 5% of the value. The other 95% is the work behind the call: pulling up the policy, filing the claim, writing the result back to the core system. If AI can handle a machine caller's request at this level, no person needs to pick up, and licensed people can focus on judgment calls, like denied claims. Most carriers aren't there yet. According to KPMG International's report Unlocking AI value in insurance , only 29% of respondents use AI agents or automation for end-to-end processes. Rullo said Guardian will keep people involved in its AI processes: "We'll still have a human in the loop." For some risk profiles, he said, Guardian wants alerts on exceptions instead of reviews of every transaction. People should own the decisions. They shouldn't have to answer every call. You Can't Always Tell Who Is Calling Carriers also can't always tell if a caller is a machine or a person. Reuters reported that Meta tested having human contractors make some Muse calls without telling the other party. A Meta vice president said the test without proper disclosures "was a miss," and Reuters said Meta has rolled back that test for now. So a call that seems to come from an AI agent might actually be from a person. Zacharia told Dig-In that Muse got around Insurify's bot detection and didn't identify itself. A system designed to resolve requests can help both human and AI callers. A system that only routes calls can't. Policyholders Already Draw the Line In Liberate's September survey of 1,001 U.S. claimants, 50% said they would prefer a claim paid in 60 seconds with no human contact over talking to a person within 10 minutes and getting paid in three days. Another 41% preferred a person on the phone. Of those who chose the fast payout, 55% still want a human involved in every denial. Fast on yes. Human on no. Across the whole survey, 61% say a human must review every denial. In the same survey, 86% want to be told when AI touches their claim. A Hi Marley survey of 550 senior property and casualty decision-makers and 2,000 policyholders in the U.S. and Canada highlights the gap carriers need to close. Eighty-five percent of executives think AI will build customer trust, but only 40% of policyholders agree. Ninety percent of policyholders said it's very or extremely important to know when they're interacting with AI, and two-thirds said their biggest worry is not being able to reach a human when it matters. Three Rules for Carriers First, use insurance-specific AI that works within your core systems to answer calls from machines. Sending a bot to a phone menu or a person wastes time and doesn't solve the problem. Second, keep a licensed person on every denial, no matter what else the AI handles. Third, be transparent about AI on both sides. Let people know when they're talking to AI, and expect AI callers to do the same. If carriers follow these rules, they can answer every call, whether it's from a person or an AI. The shopper using a machine gets a response, and the family with a flooded basement gets to talk to a real person. Insurance has always wanted to answer everyone who calls. Now it can. Amrish Singh

items.title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.original_title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.rss_title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.rss_description: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms Data Analytics ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:06 Insurers aren't avoiding AI due to fear—they're waiting for core platform vendors to deliver native capabilities instead of risky integrations. October 22, 2026 Image We've all heard some version of the same story this year: Many carriers and brokers are still on the fence about AI because of regulatory risk, errors and omissions (E&O) exposure, or "black boxes" they can't explain to a state department of insurance (DOI) examiner. All of this is true. But none of it tells the whole story. Spend time with almost any carrier's IT and operations leaders, and eventually they'll say the quiet part out loud: They're not avoiding AI; they're waiting for it to arrive inside the systems they already run. Those systems are the core platforms, such as Duck Creek, Guidewire, Majesco, Sapiens, and Insurity, that sit beneath a large share of the policies and claims on the books today. The Real Bottleneck Isn't Fear. It's Architecture. For most carriers, policy, billing, and claims data live in a core system: a multi-year, multimillion-dollar investment that the business treats as its "single source of truth." The vendor varies from carrier to carrier, but the obstacle their IT teams face is the same. Bolting a standalone AI tool onto that architecture, even an elegant and streamlined one, isn't a plug-and-play decision. It's a multi-team integration project that typically stretches across several quarters, exposing the organization to delays, cost overruns, and shifting priorities. One claims technology vendor estimates that AI vendors lose roughly 40% of their projected timelines to integration complexity, whether the carrier runs Guidewire, Duck Creek, Majesco, or a custom legacy core. That kind of complexity is often the difference between a pilot that launches and one that quietly dies in the backlog. Naturally, carriers also scan the standalone AI market. They see dozens of point solutions for underwriting triage, claims scoring, and first notice of loss (FNOL) intake, and wonder: "Why integrate a third-party layer today when the core vendor is about to deliver the same capabilities natively?" It isn't a hypothetical question. Nearly every major core platform vendor is moving to close this gap. Consider a few examples: Duck Creek launched its Agentic AI Platform in April 2026. That same month, Guidewire embedded ProNavigator, an AI assistant that gives adjusters context-specific guidance, into ClaimCenter and its other core applications. In August, Guidewire followed with its Qusar release, which added Guidewire-built claims and underwriting agents, including an agentic FNOL tool. Majesco announced that it's quadrupling its AI investment in 2026 to build an AI-native P&C platform and expand Majesco Copilot and its agentic AI capabilities. Sapiens has been rolling AI-based functionality into its CoreSuite releases. Insurity has committed an additional $100 million over two years to embed AI in its core systems, on top of the more than $50 million it had already invested in AI and R&D. In each case, the pitch is essentially the same: The AI isn't a separate purchase; it's part of the system carriers already pay for. That point is missing from many of the "why insurers are hesitant" stories in the media. Carriers aren't approaching AI cautiously simply because they're risk-averse. They're using their position as large, long-term platform customers to create a buyer's advantage. That leverage lets them be deliberate about their "build-versus-buy-versus-wait" calculations—and for many carriers, waiting has so far proved the more disciplined option. Why Waiting Is a Deceptively Difficult Decision The problem is that waiting has a cost, too, and that cost doesn't fall evenly. One AI underwriting vendor that sells a core-agnostic product has argued that carriers and managing general agents (MGAs) can't afford to wait for a full core system transformation before deploying AI and can't afford to be locked into a tool that works with only one platform. Both concerns are valid, which makes waiting a strategic bet rather than an obvious answer. There's also a quieter signal that undercuts the "carriers are simply being cautious" narrative. A May 2026 IA Capital Group survey of national and regional carriers found OpenAI's models in 91% of respondents' AI stacks, often delivered through Microsoft Copilot. Carriers aren't AI-averse. They're AI-selective, using their scale to adopt productivity tools quickly while holding the line on systems of record until their core vendors catch up. For many of them, that moment has either arrived or is very close. The Exception That Proves the Rule So why do carriers buy standalone tools at all? Because when a tool solves a problem that general-purpose AI, or the AI now arriving in core platforms, doesn't handle well, the calculus flips. That's where most insurance-specific AI vendors stake their pitch: not "we're AI," but "we're AI trained on insurance data and workflows, which a horizontal model wrapped around your files isn't." It's an argument that still holds water. Shift Technology has made this case to carrier IT leaders directly, arguing that generic horizontal AI players often lack the data foundations and expertise needed to move a pilot into production. It's a real distinction, not just positioning. A general-purpose model can summarize a claims file. Reasoning reliably across coverage language, state-specific regulations, and loss histories is a different problem, and it's one that a system trained specifically on that data is, at least in theory, built to solve. What sustains the "insurance-specific always beats generic" argument, then? The products carriers keep buying from these vendors, despite their preference for waiting until such capabilities arrive inside a core system, share one trait: They're widely believed to do the job better because of deep domain training, proprietary data, or a workflow too specialized for a core vendor to prioritize anytime soon. Everything else, such as a general chat interface bolted onto a claims queue, is the kind of functionality most likely to show up natively in the next core release, whichever vendor delivers it. That's why carriers aren't rushing to pay for it twice. What This Means If You're Evaluating Tools Right Now A few things are worth doing before you sign anything: Separating "edge" AI from "core" AI. Marketing copy and service-desk triage carry low regulatory exposure and can run successfully on general-purpose tools today. Underwriting and claims determinations that touch policyholder outcomes are a different risk category, where the wait-for-native instinct makes more sense. Asking vendors for proof of successful integrations, not just a demo. A clean demo says nothing about how a tool behaves once it's wired into a decade-old core system. Ask for a named carrier reference on your exact platform and version. Pushing for a real audit trail. If a vendor can't produce output in a format that your internal compliance team and state DOI examiners would accept, that's a governance gap that will surface at the worst possible time. Ensuring pilot programs don't require a multi-year lock-in. Any AI vendor worth considering should be comfortable running a three- to six-month pilot on a limited book of business before asking for a long-term commitment. Watching your core vendor's product roadmap as closely as the pitch deck. If your platform vendor plans to deliver the capability you're evaluating in its next release cycle, that changes the decision, even if the standalone tool works well today. Testing whether the value is domain-specific. James Ballot Diane Brassard October 22, 2026 We've all heard some version of the same story this year: Many carriers and brokers are still on the fence about AI because of regulatory risk, errors and omissions (E&O) exposure, or "black boxes" they can't explain to a state department of insurance (DOI) examiner. All of this is true. But none of it tells the whole story. Spend time with almost any carrier's IT and operations leaders, and eventually they'll say the quiet part out loud: They're not avoiding AI they're waiting for it to arrive inside the systems they already run. Those systems are the core platforms, such as Duck Creek, Guidewire, Majesco, Sapiens, and Insurity, that sit beneath a large share of the policies and claims on the books today. The Real Bottleneck Isn't Fear. It's Architecture. For most carriers, policy, billing, and claims data live in a core system: a multi-year, multimillion-dollar investment that the business treats as its "single source of truth." The vendor varies from carrier to carrier, but the obstacle their IT teams face is the same. Bolting a standalone AI tool onto that architecture, even an elegant and streamlined one, isn't a plug-and-play decision. It's a multi-team integration project that typically stretches across several quarters, exposing the organization to delays, cost overruns, and shifting priorities. One claims technology vendor estimates that AI vendors lose roughly 40% of their projected timelines to integration complexity, whether the carrier runs Guidewire, Duck Creek, Majesco, or a custom legacy core. That kind of complexity is often the difference between a pilot that launches and one that quietly dies in the backlog. Naturally, carriers also scan the standalone AI market. They see dozens of point solutions for underwriting triage, claims scoring, and first notice of loss (FNOL) intake, and wonder: "Why integrate a third-party layer today when the core vendor is about to deliver the same capabilities natively?" It isn't a hypothetical question. Nearly every major core platform vendor is moving to close this gap. Consider a few examples: Duck Creek launched its Agentic AI Platform in April 2026. That same month, Guidewire embedded ProNavigator, an AI assistant that gives adjusters context-specific guidance, into ClaimCenter and its other core applications. In August, Guidewire followed with its Qusar release, which added Guidewire-built claims and underwriting agents, including an agentic FNOL tool. Majesco announced that it's quadrupling its AI investment in 2026 to build an AI-native P&C platform and expand Majesco Copilot and its agentic AI capabilities. Sapiens has been rolling AI-based functionality into its CoreSuite releases. Insurity has committed an additional $100 million over two years to embed AI in its core systems, on top of the more than $50 million it had already invested in AI and R&D. In each case, the pitch is essentially the same: The AI isn't a separate purchase it's part of the system carriers already pay for. That point is missing from many of the "why insurers are hesitant" stories in the media. Carriers aren't approaching AI cautiously simply because they're risk-averse. They're using their position as large, long-term platform customers to create a buyer's advantage. That leverage lets them be deliberate about their "build-versus-buy-versus-wait" calculations—and for many carriers, waiting has so far proved the more disciplined option. Why Waiting Is a Deceptively Difficult Decision The problem is that waiting has a cost, too, and that cost doesn't fall evenly. One AI underwriting vendor that sells a core-agnostic product has argued that carriers and managing general agents (MGAs) can't afford to wait for a full core system transformation before deploying AI and can't afford to be locked into a tool that works with only one platform. Both concerns are valid, which makes waiting a strategic bet rather than an obvious answer. There's also a quieter signal that undercuts the "carriers are simply being cautious" narrative. A May 2026 IA Capital Group survey of national and regional carriers found OpenAI's models in 91% of respondents' AI stacks, often delivered through Microsoft Copilot. Carriers aren't AI-averse. They're AI-selective, using their scale to adopt productivity tools quickly while holding the line on systems of record until their core vendors catch up. For many of them, that moment has either arrived or is very close. The Exception That Proves the Rule So why do carriers buy standalone tools at all? Because when a tool solves a problem that general-purpose AI, or the AI now arriving in core platforms, doesn't handle well, the calculus flips. That's where most insurance-specific AI vendors stake their pitch: not "we're AI," but "we're AI trained on insurance data and workflows, which a horizontal model wrapped around your files isn't." It's an argument that still holds water. Shift Technology has made this case to carrier IT leaders directly, arguing that generic horizontal AI players often lack the data foundations and expertise needed to move a pilot into production. It's a real distinction, not just positioning. A general-purpose model can summarize a claims file. Reasoning reliably across coverage language, state-specific regulations, and loss histories is a different problem, and it's one that a system trained specifically on that data is, at least in theory, built to solve. What sustains the "insurance-specific always beats generic" argument, then? The products carriers keep buying from these vendors, despite their preference for waiting until such capabilities arrive inside a core system, share one trait: They're widely believed to do the job better because of deep domain training, proprietary data, or a workflow too specialized for a core vendor to prioritize anytime soon. Everything else, such as a general chat interface bolted onto a claims queue, is the kind of functionality most likely to show up natively in the next core release, whichever vendor delivers it. That's why carriers aren't rushing to pay for it twice. Marketing copy and service-desk triage carry low regulatory exposure and can run successfully on general-purpose tools today. Underwriting and claims determinations that touch policyholder outcomes are a different risk category, where the wait-for-native instinct makes more sense. Asking vendors for proof of successful integrations, not just a demo. A clean demo says nothing about how a tool behaves once it's wired into a decade-old core system. Ask for a named carrier reference on your exact platform and version. Pushing for a real audit trail. If a vendor can't produce output in a format that your internal compliance team and state DOI examiners would accept, that's a governance gap that will surface at the worst possible time. Ensuring pilot programs don't require a multi-year lock-in. Any AI vendor worth considering should be comfortable running a three- to six-month pilot on a limited book of business before asking for a long-term commitment. Watching your core vendor's product roadmap as closely as the pitch deck. If your platform vendor plans to deliver the capability you're evaluating in its next release cycle, that changes the decision, even if the standalone tool works well today. If a vendor's edge could be replicated by connecting a general-purpose model (for example, an enterprise assistant such as Microsoft Copilot, or an AI workflow that retrieves and summarizes documents) to your own policy forms, endorsements, claim files, and underwriting guidelines, don't count on that edge lasting once your core system catches up. items.rss_description: The Insurance Alignment Gap: Where Insurer Priorities and Customer Protection Needs Converge…and Diverge Emerging Technologies RyanMeyer Wed, 10/21/2026 - 10:47 Insurers are modernizing for efficiency, while customers seek affordability, trust, and protection. This report reveals how closing the alignment gap can create lasting value. October 21, 2026 Image Insurers are prioritizing cost reduction, profitability, modernization, and AI. Customers are looking for something different: affordability, trust, preparedness, and protection that feels relevant to the risks they face every day. This growing alignment gap matters. Modernization and AI investments deliver their full value only when customers see and feel the benefit. When insurer priorities and customer expectations drift apart, confidence erodes, and so does the opportunity to help customers build financial resilience. Based on original research with both insurers and insurance customers, this report examines where priorities align, where they diverge, and how insurers can connect business transformation to customer value. It explores three areas that matter most to building confidence and resilience: Relevance. Customers want protection that reflects their everyday risks. Learn how insurers can deliver coverage that feels meaningful and worth the cost. Personalization. Tailored products, pricing, and communications help customers feel understood and prepared. Learn how personalization supports trust. Digital engagement. Digital experiences shape how customers perceive their insurer. Learn how to use them to strengthen confidence and connection. Whether you lead strategy, product, distribution, customer experience, or technology, this report offers a research-based view of what customers expect and how your transformation priorities can meet them. Read the Report Sponsored by Majesco ITL Partner: Majesco

Customers are looking for something different: affordability, trust, preparedness, and protection that feels relevant to the risks they face every day. This growing alignment gap matters. Modernization and AI investments deliver their full value only when customers see and feel the benefit. When insurer priorities and customer expectations drift apart, confidence erodes, and so does the opportunity to help customers build financial resilience. Based on original research with both insurers and insurance customers, this report examines where priorities align, where they diverge, and how insurers can connect business transformation to customer value. It explores three areas that matter most to building confidence and resilience: Relevance. Customers want protection that reflects their everyday risks. Learn how insurers can deliver coverage that feels meaningful and worth the cost. Personalization. Tailored products, pricing, and communications help customers feel understood and prepared. Learn how personalization supports trust. Digital engagement. Digital experiences shape how customers perceive their insurer. Learn how to use them to strengthen confidence and connection. Whether you lead strategy, product, distribution, customer experience, or technology, this report offers a research-based view of what customers expect and how your transformation priorities can meet them. items.title: Senior care liability claims grow costlier
items.original_title: Senior care liability claims grow costlier
items.rss_title: Senior care liability claims grow costlier
items.rss_description: Senior living facilities are seeing liability insurance rates stabilize amid increased capacity and competition, as they face a changing operating environment, but claims are becoming more costly, and concerns over claim severity are rising, industry sources say.
items.extracted_text: Primary general and professional liability rate increases remain relatively moderate for operators with strong risk management and favorable loss experience, but conditions are tougher in more litigious jurisdictions. Excess liability rates, particularly on large accounts, are under greater pressure, however, as insurers restrict capacity and seek double-digit rate increases. Across the senior living sector, which includes assisted living, memory care and skilled nursing facilities, operators face a growing array of liability exposures as they care for residents with increasingly complex needs. Falls and pressure injuries remain among the most frequent claims, while allegations involving resident abuse and elopement — when a resident leaves a facility or secured area unsupervised — though less frequent, can result in particularly severe losses, sources said (see chart). After a brief post-pandemic slowdown, claim severity increased sharply beginning in 2023, said Blaine Thomas, Bloomington, Minnesota-based vice president, global health care — technical underwriting and product development leader at CNA. Medical inflation and litigation-related factors such as large jury awards are contributing to higher claim values, he said. “It’s not all about the $10 million claims,” Mr. Thomas said. Lower-value claims that previously settled for $175,000 are now reaching anywhere up to $500,000, which creates “a significant expense burn” for this industry, he said. Recent claims data also point to rising severity. Average indemnity payments on senior care claims increased to $253,000 in 2024 from $179,000 in 2019, according to a July report from MedPro Group, a Berkshire Hathaway company. The average indemnity payment for memory care cases in assisted living facilities was $233,000, almost 23% higher than for assisted living cases with no memory care exposure, according to its analysis of more than 2,000 claims nationally. Recent jury verdicts include a $110 million award by a Sacramento County, California, jury earlier this year. The case involved a 100-year-old resident with Alzheimer’s dementia who wandered outside a senior living facility in Sacramento and died of hypothermia. The award included $100 million in punitive damages. DigitalBridge Group, formerly known as Colony Capital and a defendant in the case, said in an Aug. 4 SEC filing that it disagrees with the verdict and intends to appeal any judgment and pursue all available post-trial remedies. In July, a federal jury in Montana awarded nearly $16 million to the families of two residents of a Billings memory care and assisted living facility, including $15.5 million in punitive damages, in a case involving allegations of negligent care. Defendant Koelsch Senior Communities is seeking to reduce the punitive damages awards in post-trial motions. Senior living claims can be particularly difficult to defend because they concern vulnerable individuals and may include allegations of neglect or abuse that can generate sympathy or anger among jurors, said William J. Mundy, a health care defense attorney at Burns White in Philadelphia. Unlike many bodily injury claims, senior living cases often involve no lost wages or future medical costs, he said. Plaintiffs instead may focus on allegations of abuse or neglect and loss of dignity. “Once you hit that emotional component, and if you’re really good at it, maybe anger, then it pushes the value up,” Mr. Mundy said. Excess liability under pressure Some senior living operators are seeing double-digit rate increases for excess and umbrella liability coverage, and insurers have pulled back limits, industry sources said. Benchmark Senior Living saw roughly 20% year-over-year increases in its excess liability program at its most recent renewal, said Rachel Thuerk, vice president, risk management at the Waltham, Massachusetts-based senior living operator. The company’s primary liability program has remained relatively stable, she said. Benchmark, which has 72 senior living communities across nine states from Virginia to Maine, operates largely outside tough liability jurisdictions such as California, Cook County, Illinois, or Philadelphia, she said. Excess capacity remains available, but at a higher cost, Ms. Thuerk said. “If I see another 20% or 25% year-over-year increase on excess liability, that may change the size of our tower,” she said. Benchmark is considering retaining more of its risk through a captive, she said. The company is conducting a captive feasibility study for retained workers compensation losses, and other coverages could follow once a captive is established, she said (see related story). Excess and umbrella liability rate increases can reach 30% or more, depending on the size of the insurance tower and where capacity is sourced, said Scott Wallace, Chicago-based managing director of the senior living and long-term care industry practice at Marsh Risk. Insurers historically deployed $10 million and sometimes up to $15 million in individual excess limits, but those limits have generally been reduced to $5 million, he said. Larger excess towers typically require multiple insurers, said Jack Harms, Boca Raton, Florida-based assistant vice president and broker at CRC. A $20 million tower could require three or four insurers. “A lot of carriers start — they’re fine giving out $5 million — but once they’re putting out $10 million or more, then they start getting a little bit uneasy,” he said. Abuse coverage can also become more restrictive higher up the liability tower. Coverage is generally available, but operators should check whether excess policies follow abuse sublimits in the primary policy, Mr. Harms said. “You can think that there’s abuse coverage included in the excess, but because it’s sublimited on the primary and sublimits are excluded on the excess, all of a sudden you don’t have abuse (cover) going all the way up,” he said. Primary liability pricing remains more competitive. Rates are generally flat to up single digits for operators with good loss experience in more favorable jurisdictions, said Alex Whipple, Phoenix-based senior vice president, senior living practice at CAC, part of The Baldwin Group. California remains markedly tougher, even for operators with good loss records. Insurers may require substantially higher retentions or significant rate increases, he said. An operator with a $100,000 retention, for example, could see it increase to $250,000 despite having a favorable loss ratio, Mr. Whipple said. Some middle-market and smaller operators in markets such as California are forgoing excess liability coverage because of its cost, he said. Larger operators, however, generally continue to buy the coverage. Los Angeles and Sacramento counties remain among the toughest venues, while Cook County, Illinois, Florida and Georgia are also challenging, he said. Claim severity has been increasing at a compounded rate of about 10% on primary coverage, while rate increases since 2023 have not kept pace, said Mr. Thomas at CNA. “The marketplace has undershot that severity trend,” he said. Focus turns to risk management Senior living operators are increasingly turning to technology to prevent falls and manage risk, industry sources say. Benchmark Senior Living has been testing SafelyYou, an AI-powered camera system that detects falls, in several of its memory care communities, said Ms. Thuerk. The system can help staff determine what happened during an incident, including whether a resident struck their head, lowered themselves to the floor or recovered without assistance, she said. The video provides a record of what happened and helps staff determine the appropriate response, such as whether a resident needs to be transferred to an emergency room, Ms. Thuerk said. Benchmark has also increased in-person staff training in areas including wheelchair securement, elopement prevention, chemical security and fire safety. “Sending somebody a video that they click through and hit the button at the end, and you say, ‘Check, you’re trained.’ Very little of that gets retained versus in-person, physical, hands-on training,” she said. Staffing, adherence to protocols and communication issues were overrepresented in paid senior living claims with payments of $500,000 or more, according to MedPro. Insurers are also scrutinizing senior living ownership structures, including whether private equity is involved and whether facilities have changed hands repeatedly, said Dan Gilhooly, managing director, senior living practice at Arthur J. Gallagher & Co. in Rolling Meadows, Illinois. “Who actually operates these? What’s the tenure that these individuals have owned and operated the buildings? And then, who’s calling the shots?” he said. Frequent ownership or management changes can raise questions about leadership and staffing stability, while new equity investment could be viewed favorably when it brings an experienced owner and additional investment in a facility, Mr. Gilhooly said. Insurers have been slower to translate the use of loss-prevention technology into specific premium discounts, said Carl Swan, Phoenix-based executive vice president, senior living practice at CAC. Some systems, for example, immediately alert nurses through their phones if a resident may be falling, he said. For larger insurance programs, insurers may instead provide $25,000 to $50,000 risk management grants that can help fund fall-prevention, wound-care or predictive-analytics technology, Mr. Swan said. Alternative risk transfer vehicles make inroads in tough sector Senior living operators are exploring alternative risk financing options, such as captive insurers and risk retention groups, as claims severity rises and large jury verdicts pressure the sector, industry sources say. Interest in captives and risk retention groups has increased, said Julie Bordo, CEO of PCH Mutual, a Vermont-based risk retention group. PCH was formed in 2004 to provide liability coverage to small and midsize nonmedical residential care facilities, which historically had limited options for affordable, comprehensive insurance, she said. The RRG, which operates in 47 states, most commonly provides limits of $1 million per occurrence and $3 million aggregate and also provides sexual and physical abuse coverage. “For a long time, there wasn’t a lot else out there for them that offered comprehensive insurance at all or at a reasonable price,” Ms. Bordo said. PCH also provides members with risk management resources, including documentation software designed to help facilities maintain records of resident care, she said. The services are available at no cost to members. Group captive options have also expanded. In January, Marsh Agency launched Secure Harbor, a group captive offering general and professional liability coverage to skilled nursing, assisted living and senior living facilities. Domiciled in Washington, D.C., Secure Harbor offers general and professional liability coverage with limits up to $1 million per occurrence and $3 million in aggregate to senior living services businesses with similar risk profiles. Members have access to Marsh Agency’s third-party administrator services team and safety consulting experts. The senior living sector has shifted significantly toward greater risk retention over the past decade, said Blaine Thomas, Bloomington, Minnesota-based vice president, global health care — technical underwriting and product development leader at CNA. About 90% of insurance premium in the sector is now tied in some way to a deductible or self-insured retention, compared with a market that was once predominantly first-dollar coverage, he said. Some larger operators are also using captive arrangements as they retain more liability risk, including fronted and matching-deductible structures, Mr. Thomas said. “Some insureds are shifting and building towers. items.extracted_text: Liberty Mutual Re and Celest.Science explore parametric trigger data fallback - Artemis.bm Liberty Mutual Re and Celest.Science explore parametric trigger data fallback - Artemis.bm Liberty Mutual Re and Celest.Science explore parametric trigger data fallback 26th October 2026 - Author: Jack Willard Liberty Mutual Reinsurance (LM Re) part of Liberty Mutual Insurance Group, and Celest.Science have announced a collaboration to explore the development of a potential fallback methodology intended to support event characterisation for parametric tropical cyclone insurance when crucial weather data is either unavailable or delayed. Parametric insurance provides payment when pre-agreed parameters relating to an event, such as a storm’s track, footprint or intensity are met, rather than by reference to assessed loss. However the speed and transparency of this highly depends on having access to trusted sources of data. With this in mind, LM Re is exploring alternative approaches to ensure data continuity within an evolving risk landscape when access to essential observational inputs is disrupted. As per the announcement, the collaboration between the two companies will explore how LM Re’s parametric risk transfer expertise and Celest.Science’s climate modelling capabilities can be combined to develop and test a potential missing data methodology. Celest.Science offers deep levels of expertise in climate intelligence, applying AI, climate physics and advanced modelling to fill gaps where observational data remains limited. Liberty Mutual Re noted that this collaboration aligns with its broader commitment of working with prominent scientific and technology partners to drive further innovation across its parametric portfolio. “The proposed methodology would draw on multiple independent data streams alongside advanced physical and statistical modelling to characterise tropical cyclones, even when one or more traditional data sources are unavailable,” LM Re and Celest.Science explained. The companies further noted that by reducing dependence on any single data source, the proposed approach aims to support confidence, objectivity and operational continuity in event characterisation. Additionally, the collaboration will assess its potential to strengthen the resilience of parametric insurance and support fast and transparent claims settlement for clients when they need it most. Importantly, LM Re stated that any future use of the methodology in one of the firm’s products will be subject to successful technical validation, applicable governance approvals and the terms of the relevant insurance or reinsurance contract. Jean-Christophe Garaix, Head of Parametrics & Agriculture, LM Re, said: “As the risk landscape evolves and the availability of critical observational data becomes increasingly uncertain, LM Re continues to explore innovative approaches intended to enhance the robustness of its parametric products. When a tropical cyclone strikes, our clients need timely access to funds so they can focus on recovery. Our collaboration with Celest.Science enables us to explore options that could provide that extra layer of resilience, even if a primary data source becomes unavailable.” Léo Lemordant, Co-Founder and CEO, Celest.Science, said: “Extreme weather often unfolds where observations are fragmented or incomplete. By combining climate science, physics-based modelling and AI, we aim to explore how we can reconstruct a robust picture of what happened. Working with Liberty Mutual Re allows us to explore how that capability could support greater resilience in parametric insurance for end users. This collaboration between LM Re and Celest.Science is particularly interesting given that parametric catastrophe bonds always have a fallback data provider, or source specified in the bond’s terms. However, with parametric insurance, this doesn’t always seem to be the case. Therefore, identifying ways to utilise additional data sources to create formal fallback data providers for trigger settlement would be highly valuable for the parametric re/insurance market. items.extracted_text: Hannover Re secures 125% upsized $450m Acorn Re parametric cat bond - Artemis.bm Hannover Re secures 125% upsized $450m Acorn Re parametric cat bond - Artemis.bm Hannover Re secures 125% upsized $450m Acorn Re parametric cat bond 26th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Hannover Re’s seventh catastrophe bond offering in the annual Acorn Re parametric US earthquake series of deals has now been successfully priced at the bottom of initial guidance, to secure a 125% upsized $450 million of reinsurance limit from the Acorn Re Ltd. (Series 2026-1) cat bond issuance, Artemis has learned. Hannover Re came back to market with this new and now seventh Acorn Re parametric catastrophe bond earlier this month , initially seeking $200 million of risk transfer and reinsurance limit for the single named ceding insurer, Oak Tree Assurance Ltd. while also sourcing additional protection to cover other reinsurance deals it has entered into. As we reported in a first update on this new cat bond, the offering size had initially been increased by 75% to seek $350 million of limit, while the price guidance was lowered . Then, in our second update on the cat bond offering, the target size was further increased, with $450 million of parametric earthquake reinsurance limit being sought and at the same time the price guidance was reduced again. Now, we’ve learned from sources that the notes were successfully priced at the end of last week, to secure the now 125% upsized $450 million of parametric earthquake reinsurance limit priced at the bottom of the initial guidance range. Acorn Re parametric earthquake cat bonds have now been issued four years in a row, as this deal becomes an increasingly regular and annual feature of this time of year. Read about all seven Acorn Re issuances in our catastrophe bond Deal Directory . We won’t repeat all the details of the cat bond in our updates on size and pricing, so be sure to visit the Deal Directory entry for more background on the transaction . With the notes now priced and the deal finalised, Bermuda-based special purpose insurer (SPI) Acorn Re Ltd. will issue and sell a $450 million tranche of Series 2026-1 Class A cat bond notes to investors. The proceeds of the sale will fully-collateralize a parametric reinsurance agreement to fund protection for the Kaiser Permanente captive, Oak Tree Assurance, as well as for certain exposures in the covered area that Hannover Re has written for its cedent clients. The notes will provide per-occurrence based parametric reinsurance protection against earthquakes that strike the U.S. west coast region across a three year term, with the main focus of the parametric reinsurance protection being earthquakes in California, but the parametric trigger grid or box structure covering neighbouring states as well. What was initially a $200 million tranche of Acorn Re 2026-1 Class A notes were first increased to $350 million, before they increased again to $450 million in size terms, which is where the offering was finalised. The Acorn Re 2026-1 Class A cat bond notes come with an initial expected loss of 0.78%. They were first offered to cat bond investors with price guidance for an initial risk interest spread of between 2% to 2.25%, which was lowered at the first update to between 2% and 2.15% and then again to a range of 1.9% to 2% at the second update. We’re now told the $450 million of notes have been priced to pay investors an initial risk interest spread of 2%, so not quite at the lowest-end of guidance but at the lowest-end of the initially offered range. It’s another example of strong catastrophe bond price execution in the current softened reinsurance market environment, but perhaps encouraging the spread did not fall to the lowest-end as investors demanded a minimum rate of return for the risk they will be assuming. We can compare the pricing to the Acorn Re 2025-1 cat bond from roughly one year ago, which had an initial expected loss of 0.96% and priced to pay investors a spread of 2.35%, so with a multiple-at-market of 2.45 times the EL. These new 2026-1 notes from Acorn Re have now priced with a multiple-at-market of 2.56 times the expected loss, so actually slightly higher. That’s unlikely a reflection of any change in the pricing environment, we believe, more so a reflection of the lower EL risk level and investors minimum return requirements. You can read all about this new Acorn Re Ltd. (Series 2026-1) transaction and every other catastrophe bond in the Artemis Deal Directory . items.extracted_text: VW Plans New $4B Audi Plant in Georgia Article 0 Comments Volkswagen AG plans to build a new $4 billion factory for its premium Audi brand in the southern US state of Georgia, expecting the move will yield potential relief from tariffs that have severely eroded profits. The German manufacturer will build a new plant in Macon, central Georgia, to make large SUVs including the new Q9 and Q5 that’s currently manufactured in Mexico, Audi said Saturday. Construction of the greenfield project will start next year with a capacity to produce about 200,000 vehicles per year. President Donald Trump on Saturday called the plan “incredible,” saying it was a testament to the impact tariffs levied by the US on auto imports are having. The move, set to create 4,500 jobs, heralds a political win for Trump in the final stretch of the midterm election cycle. Unlike competitors BMW AG and Mercedes-Benz Group AG, Audi relies exclusively on imports from Europe and Mexico into the US, making it subject to Trump’s punishing tariffs. Its top-selling Q5 SUV is hit particularly hard because it doesn’t comply with the USMCA, the trade pact with Canada and Mexico Trump negotiated in his first term. Audi’s US sales were down 16% this year through September. “Audi can only be successful if we have a global footprint,” Audi Chief Executive Officer Gernot Döllner said Sunday during a call with reporters, adding that Audi is currently loss-making in the world’s second-biggest auto market. “By investing here, we’ll make our business model more robust.” Parent VW still needs to finalize the plan for the facility. Its powerful worker representatives, which make up half the supervisory board, signaled they may extract concessions to greenlight the factory during difficult labor, wage and investment talks in Germany. Döllner said he expected a decision by VW’s supervisory board next month. The company has been through a bruising few months as management and workers clashed over measures to boost competitiveness that at one point targeted plant closures in Germany. Last month, VW won an agreement to double global job cuts to 100,000, or roughly 15% of its workforce. “Additional production in new location always has to complement and benefit existing sites in the global production network,” VW’s works council said Sunday in an email. “In this respect, there are several open questions yet to be answered internally through relevant committees.” Europe’s biggest carmaker has considered adding another American manufacturing site on and off for years, including dating back to 2018 during Trump’s first term. Audi had repeatedly delayed a decision, with VW CEO Oliver Blume saying the group cannot afford to pay high tariffs and heavily invest in new production capacity at the same time. In exchange for the factory commitment, Trump and VW will keep holding talks on some kind of tariff reprieve, a US official involved in the negotiations said Saturday. Any changes would apply to all manufacturers who expand US production, not just Volkswagen and its brand. Talks are focused on a potential deal that would give some sort of proportional tariff relief credit to manufacturers that bring concrete commitments of new production to the US, the official said. On Sunday, Döllner declined to comment on potential future tariff relief. Selecting Georgia places Audi’s new plant in one of America’s foremost political battleground states, creating an incentive for both Democrats and Republicans to back the deal, or at least not upend it. Trump is traveling across the country in a pre-voting campaign blitz, even as polls show his popularity at or near all-time lows and Republicans facing the prospect of a sizeable defeat on Nov. 3. It generally takes years to build a new auto assembly plant, and Audi expects the first models to roll off the production line in the early 2030s. VW, which owns Audi and Porsche, is trying to reset a US business that’s long fallen short of its ambitions. Blume has identified North America as one of VW’s biggest remaining growth opportunities, particularly for rugged SUVs and pickups that produce large profits, and where the group has little presence. It’s also grappling with waning sales in China, which had long been a key source of growth and earnings for the German carmaker. “We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs and produce them here in Macon,” Döllner said at Saturday’s rally, standing near Trump. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.” Audi plans to introduce the Q9 in the US this year, its biggest SUV and one aimed at winning market share from models like the Mercedes GLS and General Motors Co.’s Cadillac Escalade. The new model will be made in Slovakia, though, meaning it too would be subject to Trump’s auto tariffs. Volkswagen also owns a factory in Tennessee that was organized by the United Autoworkers Union in 2024, and is building a plant in South Carolina that will produce Scout Terra SUVs and Traveler pickups. Audi has previously signaled that making vehicles at the latter facility would be an option. Copyright 2026 Bloomberg. Topics Georgia Was this article valuable? items.extracted_text: FEMA Launches Online Purchasing for Flood Insurance Policies Article 0 Comments The Federal Emergency Management Agency said it has launched a new tool for residents to buy flood insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program. Available, at floodsmart.gov, the online option is available to residents living in the almost 22,700 NFIP communities across the country. “We are making it easier for people to reduce their financial risk and protect what they’ve spent their lives building,” said FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton, in a statement on Oct. 20. “With this new digital tool, you can get a quote and buy a flood insurance policy in a matter of minutes.” Homeowners can get a free quote after entering information such as address, foundation type, construction type, elevation, and location of HVAC systems. Customers can purchase online or take the quote to an agent. The portal can provide contact information for three licensed insurance agents in the customer’s state. Related: National Flood Insurance Program’s Authority to Expire in December Flood damage is not covered by standard homeowners and renters insurance policies. Homeowners with federally backed mortgages who live in a designated flood zone are required to buy flood insurance. Coverage is available from the NFIP, administered by FEMA, as well as from the providers in the private insurance market. NFIP provides coverage for up to $250,000 for the home structure and $100,000 for personal possessions. According to a recent report from the Government Accountability Office, 86% of at-risk properties do not have NFIP coverage as of April 2026. The number of NFIP policies declined from 5.5 million in 2010 to 4.5 million in 2026, with the private market offsetting some of the decline. The GOA said many properties remain at-risk because FEMA’s flood zones do not account for all flood risks, such as from heavy rainfall. Was this article valuable? items.extracted_text: Avec 11,5 milliards d’euros de cotisations en août 2026, l’assurance vie demeure un levier essentiel pour financer l’économie française et européenne - France Assureurs À 11,5 milliards d’euros, les cotisations en assurance vie sont en baisse de −6 % en août 2026 par rapport au même mois de 2025. Les prestations du mois d’août 2026 s’élèvent à 9,5 milliards d’euros, en hausse de +15 % par rapport à août 2025. Elles atteignent ainsi leur plus haut niveau depuis trois ans pour un mois d’août. La collecte nette s’établit à +2,0 milliards d’euros, en baisse de −1,9 milliard d’euros par rapport à celle d’août 2025. Depuis le début de l’année, elle s’élève à +43,5 milliards d’euros, supérieure de +6,9 milliards d’euros à celle de 2025 sur la même période. En août 2026, les cotisations en assurance vie s’élèvent à 11,5 milliards d’euros, en diminution de −6 % par rapport au même mois de 2025 où les cotisations avaient atteint un niveau exceptionnellement élevé (12,2 milliards d’euros, soit +27 % par rapport à août 2024). Les cotisations progressent de +3 % pour les supports en unités de compte (UC) mais diminuent pour les supports en euros (−10 %). Depuis début 2026, les cotisations atteignent 138,7 milliards d’euros, en hausse de +9,2 milliards d’euros, soit +7 % par rapport aux huit premiers mois de 2025. Cette dynamique positive concerne principalement les supports en UC (+10 %) et dans une moindre mesure ceux en euros (+5 %). La part des UC dans les cotisations s’établit à 37 % sur le mois d’août 2026 et se maintient à 40 % sur les huit premiers mois de l’année. À 9,5 milliards d’euros, les prestations du mois d’août 2026 sont en hausse de +15 % par rapport à août 2025. Cette augmentation est portée essentiellement par les supports en UC (+27 %), tandis que ceux en euros enregistrent une hausse de +11 %. Les prestations atteignent ainsi leur plus haut niveau pour un mois d’août depuis trois ans, avec notamment 2,4 milliards d’euros de prestations sur les supports en UC. Depuis le début de l’année, les prestations s’élèvent à 95,2 milliards d’euros, en légère progression de +2,3 milliards d’euros, soit +2 % par rapport aux huit premiers mois de 2025. Cette dynamique concerne principalement les supports en UC qui augmentent de +1,5 milliard d’euros, tandis que les prestations des supports en euros sont en hausse de +0,8 milliard d’euros. La collecte nette s’établit donc à +2,0 milliards d’euros en août 2026. Les supports en UC représentent l’essentiel de cette dynamique, avec une collecte nette positive de +1,9 milliard d’euros, tandis que les supports en euros enregistrent une collecte positive de +0,2 milliard d’euros. Depuis le début de l’année, la collecte nette s’élève à +43,5 milliards d’euros, supérieure de +6,9 milliards d’euros à celle de 2025 sur la même période. Les supports en UC concentrent une partie très majoritaire de cette collecte nette (+33,9 milliards d’euros), tandis que ceux en euros y contribuent à hauteur de +9,7 milliards d’euros. L’encours des contrats d’assurance vie atteint 2 171 milliards d’euros à fin août 2026, en hausse de +5,7 % sur un an (+117 milliards d’euros). Selon Paul ESMEIN, directeur général de France Assureurs : «En août 2026, les cotisations en assurance vie demeurent à un niveau élevé, à 11,5 milliards d’euros. Depuis le début de l’année, la dynamique de l’assurance vie confirme la confiance des Français dans ce produit d’épargne de long terme, qui leur permet de préparer leur avenir, tout en contribuant au financement de l’économie française. Avec 80 % de ses encours investis au sein de l’Union européenne et plus de la moitié sur le territoire français, l’assurance vie constitue un levier essentiel au service de la souveraineté nationale et européenne. » Pour en savoir plus sur l’assurance vie, cliquez ici. NB : l’arrondi d’un total ou d’une différence n’est pas nécessairement égal à la somme ou à la différence des arrondis de ses composantes. C’est parfois le cas entre la collecte nette d’une part et la différence entre les cotisations et les prestations d’autre part, lorsque ces grandeurs sont toutes trois arrondies en milliards d’euros. items.extracted_text: VP Bank stays neutral on cat bonds, notes quiet hurricane season and hedging costs - Artemis.bm VP Bank stays neutral on cat bonds, notes quiet hurricane season and hedging costs - Artemis.bm VP Bank stays neutral on cat bonds, notes quiet hurricane season and hedging costs 26th October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Despite the fact premia has reduced in the catastrophe bond market, private bank and asset manager VP Bank AG maintains a neutral weighting on insurance-linked securities noting that the Atlantic hurricane season is currently running its course loss free, although also highlighting the expensive cost of currency hedging. VP Bank has remained positive on the inclusion of catastrophe bonds and ILS within investor portfolios for their diversification benefits, seeing the value persisting even as yields have declined. Yields to maturity of new catastrophe bond and ILS issuance have declined over the last three years with the softening of reinsurance pricing, which you can analyse in our chart displaying Plenum Investment’s cat bond market yield data , but for VP Bank the return potential of the asset class continues to compare favourably with other far more correlated and less diversifying investment categories . In its latest view on the markets, VP Bank highlights that it continues to maintain a neutral weighting on the ILS asset class, which means it is maintaining allocations and continues to view the independence from broader capital markets as a positive source of returns for its portfolios. On the positive side, VP Bank notes that the Atlantic hurricane season remains “extremely quiet” having seen over 80% of the season pass before the first hurricane Isaias formed. “2026 is the first season since the introduction of satellites 60 years ago to have entered October without a hurricane,” the investment firm noted. Adding that, “In the Pacific, by contrast, this was only the second time ever that three hurricanes were active simultaneously. For the cat bond market, however, this had had little impact, so far,” and noting that storms to-date there have not attached the parametric cat bond in Mexico. Also seen as positive is the fact that interest rates are rising, which of course can boost the risk-free rate of return on the collateral underpinning catastrophe bonds and other ILS instruments. On why VP Bank is neutral, rather than positive, this comes down to the fact that premia have reduced after a run of virtually claim free years. But additionally and for the first time that we’ve noticed, VP Bank also highlights the expensive cost of currency hedging associated with investments into cat bonds and ILS. Now, this does not affect all investors, but those needing to hedge currencies in certain countries can find that as spreads decline the cost of hedging begins to weigh on their decision-making with respect to an asset class like ILS. Previously VP Bank said that it views catastrophe bonds and insurance-linked securities as the “best asset class from a diversification perspective,” offering significant benefits to investors as a component of their portfolios . items.rss_title: Senator Grassley Adds to Fight for Federal TPLF Disclosure

items.extracted_text: Senator Grassley Adds to Fight for Federal TPLF Disclosure Article 0 Comments Those lobbying for changes in court rules to require disclosure of third-party litigation funding have a new ally – Sen. Chuck Grassley. Grassley, R-Iowa, the chairman of the U.S. Senate’s Judiciary Committee, submitted a letter to the Advisory Committee on Civil Rules to encourage it to amend federal rules of procedure and “increase public disclosure of third party funding in litigation.” Grassley said funders “often prioritize using the courts for monetary return rather than for obtaining justice for the parties involved in the cases.” The practice also has national security implications. He said foreign investors get involved in TPLF to learn trade secrets during the discovery process. Furthermore, companies tied up in long court battles are using funds on lawyers rather than on research and product development, Grassley wrote. “In addition to providing this data so the practice could be evaluated fairly, required disclosure would help ensure fairness in the courts,” and discourage those with “nefarious intent,” Grassley said. “If a third party funding arrangement cannot stand up to public scrutiny, it likely should not occur.” Grassley’s supports comes as little surprise. He is the sponsor of the Litigation Funding Transparency Act of 2026, which would require TPLF disclosure in multidistrict litigation, class actions, or other large cases. The Oct. 21 letter from the senator was submitted on the day of the advisory committee’s last meeting. Minutes of this meeting were not yet available but past committee gatherings of judges, lawyers, and professors indicate the topic of TPLF has come up for discussion quite often over many years. Members have distinguished the difference between evaluating TPLF’s ethicality and establishing better case management standards. The focus should be on the latter, members have said. According to comments in the minutes from an April meeting, there appears to be a fair amount of concern that any rule could account for “all of the nuances and varying circumstances of TPLF while also anticipating how rapidly the industry is changing.” In addition, any rule would need to apply to issues raised in different kinds of cases, which may vary in patent litigation versus a mass tort, for instance. The insurance industry certainly has its opinions on the matter of TPLF. The practice of investing in lawsuits in exchange for a percentage of a settlement or judgment has increased overall claims costs due to escalating litigation costs. The industry has routinely supported federal and state efforts to curtail TPLF. Insurers and its counsels were joined by others from varying industries in sending a September letter to the Advisory Committee on Civil Rules, endorsing a proposed rule endorses a rule the Lawyers for Civil Justice (LCJ) and the U.S. Chamber Institute for Legal Reform submitted to the committee to require the disclose of any funder with financial interest in the litigation, and the funding agreement. Related: Insurance Companies Join Letter to Push TPLF Disclosure in Federal Courts “Given the [rules’] emphasis on transparency about financial interests in litigation, the absence of a TPLF disclosure requirement is inexplicable,” LCJ wrote. items.original_title: Japan Takaichi Orders Cybersecurity Measures as Attacks Grow
items.rss_title: Japan Takaichi Orders Cybersecurity Measures as Attacks Grow
items.rss_description: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi ordered her cabinet to compile emergency measures by the end of next week to counter a spate of cyberattacks that have rocked Japan in recent weeks. “In response to cyberattacks whose nature has been identified, we …
items.extracted_text: Japan Takaichi Orders Cybersecurity Measures as Attacks Grow Article 0 Comments Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi ordered her cabinet to compile emergency measures by the end of next week to counter a spate of cyberattacks that have rocked Japan in recent weeks. “In response to cyberattacks whose nature has been identified, we will strategically select and implement a full range of countermeasures — including taking steps to access and neutralize the threat,” Takaichi said at an emergency ministerial meeting held Monday. She did not elaborate further on the countermeasures but asked her ministers to gather information and communicate possible risks and threats to experts, businesses and the public. Takaichi also asked her cybersecurity minister, Toshiharu Furukawa, to work closely with allies, like-minded countries and other relevant international organizations to identify the source of the attacks and to form a joint response with the international community. A recent string of data breaches has hit Japan Inc. amid concerns around the world about the use of artificial intelligence to take advantage of cybersecurity vulnerabilities. In the most recent incident for Japan, IT services provider GMO Internet Group said its foreign-exchange trading service was subject to unauthorized access, with some customers reporting transactions in their accounts that they did not recognize. On Saturday, GMO asked the government to help neutralize the source of malicious cyberactivity. Chief Executive Officer Masatoshi Kumagai said in a blog post GMO had received a demand for $50 million-worth of cryptocurrency in ransom, which it didn’t pay. The GMO incident comes less than a month after a new set of cybersecurity laws came into effect. The new framework allows for Japan to deploy “active cyber defense,” meaning that it can take a more proactive stance by identifying and eliminating emerging cybersecurity threats. The law also seeks to foster better communication and integrated countermeasures by the private and public sectors. Last week, economy minister Ryosei Akazawa said Japan plans to launch a team of so-called white hat hackers, who are cybersecurity professionals tasked with finding and fixing online security weaknesses.
